Inspect existing conditions before choosing a solution

Start with a safe, structured inspection. Do not climb onto damaged roofs, open energized equipment or modify plumbing or security hardware without the right training. Record visible conditions from safe locations and gather drawings, maintenance records, prior invoices and equipment details.

Look for patterns. Does the issue appear only after a storm, during peak occupancy, at one fixture, after a network change or in a particular season? When did it begin? Has a temporary repair changed the symptom? Pattern questions help distinguish a local defect from a system-wide problem.

Communicate expected interruptions and support contacts to occupants or staff. Keep safety procedures and official instructions available to the people performing the work.

Storms move through the Lehigh Valley faster than most homeowners expect, and what they leave behind is rarely as obvious as a hole in the roof. A storm damage roof checklist gives you a calm order to work in once the wind drops, so you catch the quiet problems before they become stained ceilings and soaked insulation.

In The Light Roofing has been working on roofs here since 2017, from Slatington and Walnutport in the north down through Northampton, Catasauqua and Coplay to Center Valley. The damage that costs the most is rarely the damage that looked worst on the day. It is the damage nobody looked for.

What Lehigh Valley Storms Actually Do to a Roof

Three things tell you most of what you need to know: visible exterior damage such as missing or damaged shingles, interior water stains on ceilings and walls, and fallen debris or tree limbs left sitting on the roof.

Wind is the quiet one. It does not have to tear a shingle off; breaking the seal between courses is enough, because the next rain then has a path underneath. Hail bruises the surface, debris punctures it, and all three can leave a roof that looks normal from the sidewalk.

Start Where It Is Safe: Inside the House

Your first look should not be from a ladder. Interior evidence is easier to read and carries no risk.

Room by room

  • Ceilings in every upstairs room, for fresh stains, rings or discoloration
  • Where walls meet ceilings, and the corners along exterior walls
  • Bubbling or peeling paint, which often shows up before a stain
  • Any new draft, damp patch or musty smell

In the attic

  • Daylight coming through the roof deck
  • Insulation that feels wet, matted or compressed
  • The underside of the decking around vents, chimneys and pipe boots
  • Rust on nail shanks, which points to repeated moisture

Walk the Perimeter Before You Look Up

What lands around your house is evidence of what left your roof. Walk the full perimeter, including the side you never use.

  • Collect shingle fragments and set them aside instead of throwing them out
  • Check gutters and downspouts for dents, separation and granule buildup
  • Look at the driveway, deck rails, siding and window screens for impact marks

Heavy granule loss points to deteriorating shingles on its own, and a storm accelerates it.

What to Check From the Ground, Looking Up

Stay off the roof. Use binoculars, or the zoom on your phone, from several angles.

  • Missing, lifted, cracked or curled shingles, especially on the windward slope
  • Ridge caps that look uneven or disturbed
  • Flashing pulled away from a chimney, wall or vent
  • Exposed underlayment showing as a lighter patch

Document Everything While It Is Fresh

Photograph what you find on the same day, from far enough back that the location is obvious and close enough that the damage is readable. Note the date of the storm and keep receipts for anything you buy to hold water back. That is what lets a roofer and an adjuster describe the same roof the same way.

Where Your House Sits Changes What You Check First

Repairs make sense when the damage is contained and the rest of the roof is still doing its job:

  • Damage limited to one slope, one penetration or one run of flashing
  • Shingles lifted or torn by wind on an otherwise sound roof
  • A leak traced to a vent boot, chimney flashing or a valley rather than the open field of the roof
  • A roof still comfortably inside its expected service life

Asphalt shingles, a popular roofing material, are known for their ease of installation and repair. Dealing with a small problem early extends the life of the roof you own and avoids the far larger expense of a premature replacement. More is on our roof repairs page.

Sometimes a patch only delays an outcome already decided. Look seriously at replacement when one of these is true:

  • Age. Roofs have a finite lifespan. When yours is reaching the end of its expected life, repairs stop being an investment and start being maintenance on something already failing.
  • Extensive or irreparable damage. Widespread leaks, saturated decking or structural movement are not repair problems.
  • Visible, general wear. Damaged shingles across the whole roof, sagging areas, and the same issue returning after every repair all say the same thing.

Our area experiences fluctuating freeze-thaw cycles that put roofs under real stress. That is repair territory more often than it looks from the sidewalk.

Ice dams are one of the few roof problems in the Lehigh Valley that build slowly enough to stop before they ever reach your ceiling. That is the case for Lehigh Valley roof ice dam prevention: the ridge of ice on your eaves does not appear overnight, and neither does the damage behind it.

At In The Light Roofing, we work on roofs across the Valley. Homeowners usually read ice at the roof edge as a shingle failure. More often the cause is above the ceiling, in the attic conditions that decide how warm the deck gets.

How Ice Dams Form on a Lehigh Valley Roof

Snow acts as insulation of its own. If the deck underneath is warmer than the outside air, the bottom layer melts, and the water runs down the slope to the eaves and gutter line, which hang past the heated part of the house and stay cold. There it refreezes, and our winters give it plenty of chances. An afternoon just above freezing followed by a night in the teens is an ordinary week here.

Repeat that and the ice builds into a ridge thick enough to block drainage. Water arriving behind it backs up under the shingle courses and finds the nail holes, the laps and the flashing. Shingles shed water running downhill. They were never built to hold back a pool.

What the Water Does Once It Is Behind the Shingles

The leak you can see is the last stage. Long before a ceiling stains, water behind a dam commonly causes:

  • Saturated attic insulation that no longer insulates
  • Mold growth in the trapped moisture above your bedrooms
  • Soft, rotting roof decking under shingles that still look intact
  • Peeling paint and stained ceilings on the top floor
  • Warped fascia and gutters pulling away from the house

Most of it happens out of sight, which is why so much surfaces in spring.

What Your Own House Brings to the Problem

An ice dam is a roof problem with a floor plan behind it, and the housing stock here gives it several shapes. If your home is one of the brick twins or rowhomes in Old Allentown or the Old Fairgrounds district, you probably have a steep pitch, a shallow overhang at the eave and almost no room between the top of the wall and the deck. Where there is a soffit to vent at all, one batt pushed too far closes it. If the top floor was finished into bedrooms, the attic meant to stay cold is now heated space.

The older borough streets in Catasauqua, Coplay and Northampton run to the same pattern: attached houses on narrow lots, draining to a front eave and a rear eave with no side slopes to take the water. Once the front eave ices over, there is no second route off the roof. And on a tree lined block like the ones in Hamilton Park, the leaves nobody got to in November are still in that gutter in January, frozen into the base of the dam.

At the north end of the Valley, Slatington and Walnutport face each other across the Lehigh River at the foot of Blue Mountain. Snow tends to sit on a roof up there rather than blow off, so the weight deserves as much attention as the ice.

Newer, larger houses around Center Valley have the opposite issue. The roof is not old, but it is complicated: cross gables, dormers, a garage wing, often a cathedral ceiling with no real attic to ventilate. Every valley there is a channel where drifted snow collects. Out around Upper Macungie, wind scours some slopes bare and loads others deep, so one side of a house can ice while the other stays clear.

Why the Fix Is Above Your Ceiling

Insulation and ventilation do two different jobs, and ice dams punish the home where one is missing. Insulation slows the heat leaving your living space. Ventilation carries off the warm, moist air that gets through, so the deck stays near the outdoor temperature. Cold air should enter low at the soffits and leave high at the ridge. Block that path and you get a warm stripe of roof, then ice at the coldest point. It is also why chipping, salting and heat cables do not hold: none of them changes why the snow melted.

What You Can Do Before the First Hard Freeze

  • Walk the attic with a flashlight, looking for frost, daylight or matted insulation
  • Check that soffit vents are open and not buried under insulation
  • Confirm bathroom and kitchen fans vent outside, not into the attic
  • Clear gutters and downspouts so the first melt can drain
  • Pull snow back from the roof edge with a roof rake, from the ground

None of that puts you on the roof. Please do not climb an iced roof yourself.

What We Look At During a Winter Roof Inspection

We start outside with a thorough examination, checking for damaged or missing shingles, signs of wear and any visible issues. Then we go inside, inspecting the attic for insulation, ventilation and water damage, and checking interior spaces for stains. You get a detailed report of our findings and recommendations, and where there is damage worth recording, we photograph it, so you have accurate information to share with your insurance provider.

When Prevention Turns Into Repair

Sometimes the ice has already won the season. Persistent leaks and water stains, cracked or curled shingles at the eave, a sagging roof deck, or granules in the gutters after the melt all point at the roof itself. Our roof repair services cover that work, from finding the source of a leak to replacing the shingles and flashing the water slipped past.

Final Thoughts: Fix the Cause, Not the Icicle

Icicles are the part that gets photographed. The cause is above your ceiling, in the balance between the heat your home loses and the air that should carry it away. If your eaves iced up last winter, they will ice up again unless something changes.

In The Light Roofing has worked on Lehigh Valley roofs since Bryson Berard opened the doors in 2017, and you are welcome to visit us in Allentown, PA to talk through your attic before the winter. If it becomes a project, we provide a no-cost estimate before you commit. Stop ice dams at the source, schedule your roof and attic inspection today.

Frequently Asked Questions

What actually causes ice dams on Lehigh Valley roofs?

Uneven roof temperature. Heat escaping into the attic melts snow up the slope, the water refreezes at the cold eaves, and the ice blocks drainage.

Do icicles always mean an ice dam?

Not always, but long or repeating icicles are worth checking, especially alongside attic frost or an upstairs ceiling stain.

Will adding insulation on its own solve it?

Rarely. They work as a pair, and adding depth while the soffit vents stay blocked leaves the attic warm.

Is it safe to remove an ice dam myself?

Stay off the roof. A roof rake used from the ground is the safe limit, and chipping or salting damages shingles and gutters.

Water is already coming through my ceiling. What now?

Contain the water, keep off the roof and call us. We will inspect the roof and attic, document what we find, and tell you which repairs are urgent.
